overview.text: Sodium chloride (NaCl), commonly called table salt, is an ionic compound in which sodium atoms transfer an electron to chlorine atoms, producing positively charged sodium ions and negatively charged chloride ions. These opposite charges attract, arranging ions in an alternating pattern that forms cubic crystals. In nature, sodium chloride occurs as the mineral halite. Salt seasons food and serves as an industrial raw material for making chlorine and caustic soda; rock salt is also spread on roads to reduce ice. Historically, salt helped preserve food through curing and became a valuable commodity, with access to deposits sometimes connected to trade and conflict.

key_facts.text: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions that attract.
Sodium and chloride ions alternate in salt crystals, which have a cubic shape.
Halite is the mineral form of sodium chloride (NaCl).
Salt is used to season food, deice roads, and manufacture chlorine and caustic soda.
Salt curing helped preserve food, and historical accounts describe disputes over access to salt deposits.
